sections.section_title: Testing the Spirits -- The Criterion of the Incarnation
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the community's obligation to test spirits by a christological criterion -- whether a spirit confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh -- in order to distinguish the Spirit of God from the spirit of the antichrist that animates the false prophets who departed the community.

sections.section_title: Two Origins, Two Audiences -- The Community's Victory Over the False Prophets
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies a binary origin scheme in which the community is 'from God' (ek tou theou) and the false prophets are 'from the world' (ek tou kosmou), with each group's origin determining its speech, its capacity to recognize truth, and the audience that receives its message.
sections.relevance: The passage presents origin as prior to and determinative of response: those who are from God listen to the apostolic testimony; those who are not from God do not. The neutral reading states: 'The community's origin determines its allegiance, its capacity to recognize truth, and its ultimate destiny.' It also states: 'Recognition of the true message is itself evidence of one's origin' and 'Non-reception of the apostolic message is evidence that the hearer is not from God.' This logic parallels the deterministic proof-texts in John 8:47 ('He who is of God hears the words of God; for this reason you do not hear them, because you are not of God') and John 10:27 ('My sheep hear my voice'), which the neutral reading itself cites as parallels. The circular structure -- those from God recognize truth because they are from God -- implies that origin precedes and governs response rather than response creating the origin. However, the passage does not directly address salvation outcomes; its immediate concern is epistemological discernment of true versus false teaching. The neutral reading also attributes the community's victory to the indwelling Spirit's superior power ('greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world'), not to the community's own choices, which further subordinates human agency to divine power in this section.
key_phrases: You are from God, little children, and have overcome them
greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world
They are from the world, therefore they speak as from the world, and the world listens to them
The one who knows God listens to us; the one who is not from God does not listen to us

sections.section_title: Love, the Nature of God, and the Incarnation as Love's Supreme Expression
sections.summary: The neutral reading traces the declaration 'God is love' through its implications: love originates in God, everyone who loves has been born of God, God's love was manifested in sending His Son as the atoning sacrifice, and the community is obligated to love one another -- with the result that if they do, God remains in them and His love is perfected in them.
sections.relevance: The passage contains elements pulling in both directions, but the dominant thrust treats human love as a genuine activity with real consequences for the divine-human relationship. The conditional in verse 12 -- 'if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us' -- presents the community's mutual love as a genuine condition for God's continuing indwelling and for love reaching its telos. The obligation language in verse 11 (opheilomen, 'we ought, we are obligated') treats love as something the community can genuinely choose to practice or neglect. The neutral reading states that God's love 'reaches its intended destination and achieves its intended purpose when the community loves one another,' making the circuit of love dependent on human participation for its completion. On the other side, verse 7's perfect tense gegennētai ('has been born of God') presents divine parentage as prior to the present act of loving, and verse 10 insists 'not that we loved God, but that He loved us' -- establishing God's love as the originating cause. However, the neutral reading interprets verse 7 as diagnostic correspondence ('the one who loves is the one who has been born of God') rather than deterministic causation, and verse 10 establishes temporal and causal priority of God's love, not the exclusion of human response. The passage's function as an exhortation to love -- which presupposes that the community can genuinely choose to love or not -- tips the balance toward human agency.
key_phrases: everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God
The one who does not love does not know God, because God is love
not that we loved God, but that He loved us
if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us
we also ought to love one another

sections.section_title: The Spirit, the Eyewitness Testimony, and Confession as the Basis of Mutual Indwelling
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents three interconnected bases for mutual indwelling with God: the gift of the Spirit as evidence of God's presence, the eyewitness testimony that the Father sent the Son as Savior of the world, and the confession that Jesus is the Son of God as the condition for God remaining in the confessor and the confessor in God.
sections.relevance: Verse 15 -- 'Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God' -- uses the indefinite construction hos ean ('whoever') with confession as the operative human act that correlates with mutual indwelling. The neutral reading identifies confession as genuine human activity with real consequences for one's relationship with God: 'The result of the confession is mutual indwelling.' The scope marker 'whoever' opens the possibility to any person who makes the confession, treating it as a genuine human act rather than a predetermined outcome for a fixed group. Meanwhile, the title 'Savior of the world' (sotera tou kosmou) in verse 14 expresses, as the neutral reading notes, 'the universal reach of God's redemptive love,' connecting to 2:2's declaration that the atonement is 'not for ours only but also for the whole world.' Universal scope of atonement implies that salvation is available to all, which coheres with human agency in responding rather than divine selection of a limited group. The Spirit as a divine gift (v. 13) reflects God's initiative, but the neutral reading presents the Spirit, confession, and mutual indwelling as interconnected aspects of the same reality rather than a deterministic chain.
key_phrases: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God
the Father has sent the Son to be the Savior of the world
He has given to us of His Spirit
We have come to know and have believed the love which God has for us

sections.section_title: God Is Love, Mutual Indwelling, and Confidence in the Day of Judgment
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the repeated declaration 'God is love' as the ground for mutual indwelling through abiding in love, with the purpose that love perfected in the community produces confidence on the day of judgment and drives out fear, since fear is oriented toward punishment and indicates that love's work is incomplete.
sections.relevance: The passage directly connects human activity (remaining in love) to salvation-relevant outcomes (confidence versus fear at the day of judgment). The conditional structure -- 'the one who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him' -- presents abiding in love as a genuine human posture with consequences for one's standing before God. The neutral reading states that 'the community that loves as God loves -- that embodies in this world the love that characterizes Jesus -- need not dread the coming judgment,' implying that the community's actual practice of love determines its posture at judgment. The diagnostic 'the one who fears is not perfected in love' treats fear as evidence that love's work is 'not yet complete,' which the neutral reading interprets as indicating an ongoing process involving human participation: 'The remedy for fear is not the suppression of emotion but the perfection of love -- the deeper experience and practice of God's love that progressively displaces fear with confidence.' The verb meno ('to remain, to abide') appearing three times in one clause emphasizes sustained human activity, not a static guarantee. The passage treats love as something humans genuinely practice, with their practice directly bearing on their experience at the final judgment.
key_phrases: the one who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him
so that we may have confidence in the day of judgment
perfect love drives out fear
the one who fears is not perfected in love
fear involves punishment

sections.section_title: The Source of Our Love and the Inseparability of Love for God and Love for the Brother
sections.summary: The neutral reading traces the community's love to God's prior love as its source and cause, then applies the final diagnostic test: the claim to love God while hating one's brother is a lie, since one who cannot love the visible brother cannot love the invisible God, and the commandment explicitly binds the two loves together as a single inseparable obligation.
sections.relevance: The passage simultaneously affirms divine initiative and genuine human responsibility. Verse 19 ('We love, because He first loved us') establishes God's temporal and causal priority -- human love is responsive, never originary. The neutral reading states: 'God's love is the cause; the community's love is the effect.' This could lean deterministic if it meant God's love automatically produces the desired response without human agency. But the diagnostic test in verses 20-21 treats love as a genuine human obligation that can be fulfilled or violated: the claim to love God while hating the brother is called a 'lie,' and the commandment binds the two loves together as something humans 'must' (dei) practice. The neutral reading's statement that 'the person who hates the visible brother is constitutionally incapable of loving the invisible God, because hatred of the brother reveals an absence of the love that comes from God' treats the absence of love as a genuine human failure with real diagnostic implications for one's standing before God -- not as evidence of predetermined exclusion but as evidence that God's love has not been genuinely received and allowed to produce its proper fruit. The 'if someone says' pattern throughout the letter consistently treats the gap between profession and conduct as a matter of human responsibility.
key_phrases: We love, because He first loved us
If someone says, 'I love God,' and yet he hates his brother or sister, he is a liar
the one who does not love his brother and sister whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen
the one who loves God must also love his brother and sister
